_comment: Carino Offline software stack. One object per piece of software you would actually deploy. `role` must match a roles[].id. `offline` is the editorial spine and takes exactly three values: "full" = keeps working indefinitely with the WAN cable pulled; "sync" = works offline but needs a periodic online refresh to stay useful (mirrors, ZIM dumps, rule feeds) — the test is whether the content ROTS without a refresh, not whether it was downloaded once. A local LLM weight file is a one-time fetch that never goes stale, so the AI stack is "full"; a CVE feed is not; "tethered" = needs a vendor account or cloud to function, listed only to warn against it or because a documented LAN-only mode exists. Every "sync" and "tethered" item MUST carry an "escape" field saying what you do about it; "full" items must not. Fields `url`, `escape`, `ram`, `disk`, `install`, `license`, `lang`, `alts` are optional — omit any field you cannot verify rather than guessing, especially `url` and `license`. Ids are unique and kebab-case. Bump `updated` (YYYY-MM) whenever licences, images or install commands are re-checked; a stale install command is the fastest way to lose a reader's trust.

roles.label: Core infrastructure
roles.blurb: DNS, certificates, time, identity, proxy — the layer everything else assumes.

roles.label: Compute & storage
roles.blurb: Hypervisor, pools, snapshots, replication. The copies that survive the fire, and the ones that do not.

roles.label: Knowledge
roles.blurb: The offline internet: encyclopedias, dev docs, web snapshots, maps, and your own paper.

roles.label: Media
roles.blurb: Video, music, photos, books. The layer that decides whether the house tolerates the rest of the plan.

roles.label: Games
roles.blurb: DRM is the enemy of offline. What still launches with the cable pulled, and what quietly does not.

roles.label: Mirrors
roles.blurb: Packages, images, ISOs. Without these an offline machine does not fail — it slowly rots.

roles.label: Communication
roles.blurb: Talking to people when the internet is gone but the people are not.

roles.label: Operations
roles.blurb: Knowing a disk is dying before the shop closes, and a landing page that works without search.

roles.label: Security & secrets
roles.blurb: Secrets, detection, encryption. Offline is not the same as absent, and it is not the same as safe.

roles.label: Local AI
roles.blurb: The offline oracle. The difference between owning a library and owning a librarian.

roles.label: Medical imaging
roles.blurb: Imaging and records on an air-gapped VLAN, where resilience and compliance turn out to be the same feature.

items.name: Authelia
items.does: Authentication portal in front of the reverse proxy: one login, per-service access rules, and TOTP two-factor.
items.why: Single sign-on that has no external identity provider anywhere in the flow — the TOTP seed lives in your database and the algorithm is arithmetic over the clock, so it works with the WAN gone (see chrony: this is where clock drift bites first). Pair it with LLDAP if you want a user directory the family can be added to; a YAML file of users is honest and sufficient below about a dozen people.
items.install: ghcr.io/authelia/authelia with configuration.yml + users_database.yml, forward_auth from Caddy

alts.note: the light user directory to put behind it (Rust, GPL-3.0)
full OIDC provider; 1 GB of RAM and an afternoon of concepts you may not need

items.name: Caddy
items.does: Reverse proxy that obtains and renews TLS certificates automatically, one short block per service.
items.why: Caddy's default is to fetch certificates from Let's Encrypt, which is a WAN dependency hiding inside a convenience feature. Point acme_ca at step-ca and the same automation becomes fully local. Nginx is faster under load and you do not have that load; Traefik is better if everything is containers and worse if half your services are not.
items.install: Caddyfile: { acme_ca https://ca.example.internal/acme/acme/directory }  then caddy run

alts.note: container-native labels; awkward for bare-metal and appliances
more moving parts, but you already know it

items.name: chrony (+ GPS/PPS)
items.does: NTP daemon that disciplines the clock, ideally against a local GPS receiver rather than a pool server on the internet.
items.why: The most underrated item in the whole stack. Cut the WAN and clocks drift; drifted clocks break TLS validation, TOTP logins, DICOM timestamps and any attempt to correlate logs across machines — and they break them three weeks later, when nobody connects the two events. A GPS/PPS hat on a Raspberry Pi is about 90 USD and removes the entire failure class. chrony over ntpd because it converges fast after a cold boot, which is what you get after a power event.
items.install: chrony.conf: refclock SHM 0 refid NMEA offset 0.5 + refclock PPS /dev/pps0 lock NMEA

alts.note: no satellites needed, drifts more, but it is 3 USD and better than nothing

items.name: step-ca
items.does: Private certificate authority with a real ACME server, so internal clients renew certificates exactly the way they renew public ones.
items.why: This is the item that decides whether HTTPS survives a block. Public certificates are capped at 47 days by 2029 and every renewal is a round trip to a CA you do not control — one filtering event and your whole intranet expires on a timer. A 10-year internal root distributed once, with ACME behind it, makes the renewal loop entirely local. The cost is real: you must get the root into every browser, phone and Java trust store in the building, and that is a day of work you will repeat for every new device.
items.install: step ca init --deployment-type standalone   # then run step-ca $(step path)/config/ca.json

alts.note: no ACME, so every renewal is manual — fine for 5 certs, miserable at 30

items.name: Technitium DNS Server
items.does: Authoritative and recursive DNS with a web GUI, split-horizon zones, DNSSEC signing, DoH/DoT server and block lists.
items.why: The whole plan rests on the same URL resolving to a LAN address inside the building and a public one outside it. Technitium does split-horizon in a form you can hand to someone else without a BIND tutorial, and it is one process instead of the Unbound+NSD pair. You pay for that with a .NET runtime and a GUI you must remember to lock down.
items.install: docker run -d --name dns -p 53:53/udp -p 53:53/tcp -p 5380:5380 technitium/dns-server

alts.note: leaner and battle-tested, but two daemons and no GUI
great blocker, weak authoritative story — it is dnsmasq underneath

items.name: Unbound
items.does: Validating, caching recursive resolver that talks to the root servers directly instead of trusting an upstream.
items.why: Put it behind Technitium as the recursor so you are not depending on 1.1.1.1 — the resolver everyone assumes is neutral is exactly the thing an order gets served to. Be honest about the limit: recursion is the one DNS function that genuinely needs the WAN. Offline it degrades to serving its cache plus whatever you wrote into local-zone.
items.install: dnf install unbound && systemctl enable --now unbound
items.escape: Anything that must resolve during a blackout belongs in an authoritative internal zone or in Unbound's local-zone/local-data, not in the cache. Ship root.hints with the box and refresh it yearly.

items.name: WireGuard
items.does: Kernel-level encrypted tunnels between sites and to an offshore relay, keyed by public keys and nothing else.
items.why: Use it for site A to site B replication and for reaching out — never let anything inside the building depend on it. The design rule is that the intranet must not notice when the overlay dies. Also know its weakness: plain WireGuard is trivially fingerprinted by DPI, so if the tunnel is your censorship path you need it over TCP/443 or behind an obfuscating transport, configured now while those are still easy to download.
items.install: wg genkey | tee private.key | wg pubkey > public.key   then wg-quick up wg0

items.name: Yggdrasil
items.does: Self-arranging encrypted IPv6 overlay where every node's address is derived from its public key.
items.why: This is the continuity path for the case DNS cannot fix: the domain is seized. An Yggdrasil address belongs to a key, not to a registrar or an allocation, so it stays valid when the zone is gone — print it on the IP card alongside the LAN literals. It also peers over plain link-local multicast, so two laptops on the same switch find each other with no infrastructure. It is an experimental network with real latency; treat it as a lifeline, not a transport.
items.install: yggdrasil -genconf > /etc/yggdrasil.conf && systemctl enable --now yggdrasil

items.name: OpenZFS
items.does: Copy-on-write filesystem with checksums, snapshots, native encryption, and send/receive replication.
items.why: Checksums are the point. Every other RAID will happily hand you a silently corrupted file and report success; ZFS tells you which file and, with RAIDZ2, fixes it. The costs are real and people discover them late: you cannot grow a RAIDZ vdev by one disk the way you grow mdadm (RAIDZ expansion landed in 2024 and is still slow and awkward), ECC memory genuinely matters, and a pool past 80% full gets noticeably slower.
items.ram: 1 GB per TB is a rule of thumb, not a requirement
items.install: zpool create -o ashift=12 tank raidz2 /dev/disk/by-id/...   then zfs create -o encryption=on tank/data

alts.note: in-kernel and flexible; RAID5/6 still not recommended for data you care about
the snapshot scheduler and replication wrapper you will want on top

items.name: par2cmdline
items.does: Generates Reed-Solomon recovery files so a damaged archive can be reconstructed from the surviving bytes.
items.why: Optical media is the layer that survives everything, and it is also the layer that develops unreadable sectors in a drawer. Ten percent PAR2 redundancy costs 10 GB on a 100 GB disc and converts most scratches and early rot from a total loss into a rebuild. Every disc that leaves the building gets SHA256SUMS and a .par2 set at the root, no exceptions — a checksum only tells you the disc is dead, PAR2 gets the data back.
items.install: par2 create -r10 -n1 archive.par2 ./*   then par2 verify archive.par2

alts.note: same format, several times faster on modern CPUs
purpose-built for optical, but effectively unmaintained

items.name: Proxmox VE
items.does: Debian-based hypervisor with LXC containers, KVM virtual machines, ZFS, snapshots and built-in replication.
items.why: The reason to run a hypervisor rather than one big Linux box is that every service becomes a snapshot you can roll back and a dataset you can zfs send to the second site. Proxmox gets you both without assembling them. Note the licence trap that is not a licence trap: the enterprise repository needs a subscription, the no-subscription repository does not, and the nag dialog is not a functional limit. Budget the subscription anyway if a client depends on the box.
items.install: Install from the ISO, then switch /etc/apt/sources.list.d to the no-subscription repository

alts.note: better storage UI, weaker virtualization story
fewer abstractions, no replication out of the box

items.name: restic
items.does: Deduplicating, encrypted, incremental backup to a local disk, an external HDD or an SFTP target.
items.why: ZFS snapshots are not backups — they die with the pool. restic is the layer that leaves the machine, and it encrypts by default so a rotated cold drive that gets lost is an inconvenience rather than a disclosure. Its verification story is what earns it a slot: restic check --read-data actually reads every byte back, which is the only way to learn that a cold drive rotted before you need it.
items.install: restic -r /mnt/cold/repo init && restic -r /mnt/cold/repo backup /srv

alts.note: faster on huge repos, but the repository format is not portable to object storage

items.name: Syncthing
items.does: Continuous peer-to-peer file synchronisation between your own devices, with no server in the middle.
items.why: The only sync tool in common use that is genuinely LAN-native: turn off global discovery and relaying and it finds peers by local multicast, so phones and laptops keep syncing with the WAN unplugged. This is the honest replacement for Dropbox in a decoupled house. It is not backup — a deletion propagates in seconds — so keep versioning on and keep restic underneath it.
items.install: docker run -d -p 8384:8384 -p 22000:22000/tcp -p 22000:22000/udp syncthing/syncthing, then disable Global Discovery and Relaying

items.name: aptly
items.does: Mirrors, snapshots and publishes Debian and Ubuntu repositories, including your own signed packages.
items.why: The snapshot model is what distinguishes it from apt-mirror: you can pin a known-good state of the archive, test against it, publish it, and roll back if an update breaks a machine — which matters far more when the fix cannot simply be re-downloaded. Mirror only the suites and architectures you actually run; a full Ubuntu LTS mirror for amd64 and arm64 is on the order of 800 GB, and most of it is packages nobody in the building will ever install.
items.disk: ~800 GB for a selective Debian/Ubuntu mirror
items.install: aptly mirror create -architectures=amd64 noble http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu noble main && aptly mirror update noble
items.escape: Refresh monthly while the WAN is up. An unmirrored security update is not a resilience problem until it is.

alts.note: much simpler, no snapshots, no publishing

items.name: devpi
items.does: Caching PyPI proxy that stores every package it has ever served and keeps serving it when upstream is unreachable.
items.why: Pull-through beats mirroring for Python: full PyPI is enormous and almost entirely irrelevant to you, whereas devpi ends up holding exactly the dependency closure your projects actually build against. Point pip at it from day one, well before you need it — a cache is only worth what passed through it, and one started during the outage is empty.
items.disk: grows with use; ~200 GB is generous
items.install: pip install devpi-server && devpi-init && devpi-server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 3141
items.escape: Set index-url in pip.conf on every machine now, and run a build of each project you care about while online so the closure is warm.

items.name: Distribution (registry:2)
items.does: The reference container registry, which in pull-through mode transparently caches every image pulled through it.
items.why: Without this, a rebooted Docker host with no WAN cannot start anything it has not already pulled, and that is the most common way a self-hosted stack dies during an outage. Two caveats worth knowing before you rely on it: a pull-through cache mirrors one upstream registry, so ghcr.io and quay.io need their own instances, and the cache does not protect you from a tag being retagged — pin digests for anything critical.
items.install: docker run -d -p 5000:5000 -e REGISTRY_PROXY_REMOTEURL=https://registry-1.docker.io registry:2
items.escape: Configure registry-mirrors in daemon.json on every host, and pull the images of every service you run at least once. Better still, docker save the critical few to a tarball on the archive disc.

alts.note: adds replication, RBAC and vulnerability scanning; also adds Postgres, Redis and real operational weight

items.name: dnf reposync + createrepo_c
items.does: Pulls a Fedora, RHEL or Rocky repository to local disk and regenerates the metadata so clients can install from it.
items.why: No extra software to run and nothing to keep alive — the mirror is a directory served by the web server you already have. Mirror the current release and n-1 only, for the one architecture you deploy; that is roughly 600 GB, versus several terabytes if you take everything. Remember --download-metadata, or you will have every package and no way for dnf to find them.
items.disk: ~600 GB for current + n-1, one architecture
items.install: dnf reposync --repoid=fedora --download-metadata -p /srv/mirror
items.escape: Re-run monthly. Keep the previous tree until the new one has been installed from successfully at least once.

items.name: Verdaccio
items.does: Lightweight npm registry that proxies the public registry, caches every tarball it serves, and hosts private packages.
items.why: The npm equivalent of devpi and the same argument applies, with more urgency: a JavaScript project's dependency tree is thousands of tarballs and any one of them missing fails the whole install. It also solves a problem that has nothing to do with censorship — a package unpublished or yanked upstream stays in your cache.
items.install: docker run -d -p 4873:4873 -v /verdaccio:/verdaccio/storage verdaccio/verdaccio
items.escape: Configure .npmrc registry on every workstation now and install each project once while online to warm the cache.

items.name: Forgejo
items.does: Self-hosted Git forge with issues, releases, LFS and a container registry, in a single Go binary.
items.why: Two jobs here. It is where every fleet repository lives locally so a seized account or a blocked host costs nothing, and it is the mirror for the 3D-print model library — every model you actually print, committed with its licence file, its sliced gcode and its printer profile. A model you cannot print during an outage is not a model you have. Pair it with git bundle for the crown-jewel discs: one self-contained, clonable file per repository.
items.install: codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:latest with a data volume; SQLite is fine below ~20 users

alts.note: the codebase Forgejo forked from; corporate governance is the only real difference

items.name: Homepage
items.does: Configurable dashboard of links and live service widgets, defined entirely in YAML files.
items.why: The landing page is what makes an intranet feel like a product instead of a list of ports, and it is the page a printed QR code should point at. One thing to fix on day one: it resolves service icons from a remote icon CDN by default, which is a WAN dependency on your offline home page. Drop the icon set into the local icons directory and reference it with sh- or the local path instead.
items.install: ghcr.io/gethomepage/homepage with config/ mounted; set HOMEPAGE_ALLOWED_HOSTS

alts.note: no widgets, no updates, never breaks — genuinely worth considering

items.name: Network UPS Tools
items.does: Reads the UPS over USB or serial and shuts hosts down cleanly in a defined order when the battery runs low.
items.why: A UPS without NUT is a device that delays the unclean shutdown by nine minutes. The part people get wrong is ordering: the storage node must be the last thing to power off and the first to come back, and the hypervisor must stop its guests before the pool goes away. Write that order down, put it in the printed runbook, and test it by actually pulling the mains — power events are the most likely outage on this whole list, well ahead of censorship.
items.install: ups.conf: driver = usbhid-ups, port = auto   then enable nut-server and nut-monitor

items.name: Prometheus + Grafana
items.does: Scrapes metrics from node_exporter and friends, stores the time series locally, and draws them.
items.why: Uptime Kuma tells you something is down; this tells you a disk has been getting slower for three weeks. That distinction is what justifies the extra complexity, and only that — if you will not look at the dashboards, run neither. One offline trap: Grafana's dashboard import and plugin catalogue both fetch from grafana.com, so provision dashboards from JSON files on disk and install plugins before you need them.
items.disk: retention-dependent; 50 GB is plenty at home scale
items.install: prom/prometheus + grafana/grafana, with prometheus/node-exporter on each host

items.name: Uptime Kuma
items.does: Status checks over HTTP, TCP, ICMP and DNS with a status page and notifications to almost anything.
items.why: Ten minutes to install and it will tell you a certificate is expiring or a container did not come back after a reboot. Two adjustments for an offline box: point the notification channel at your own Matrix or SMTP rather than a push service that needs the WAN, and add explicit monitors for the boring infrastructure — DNS answering, the CA responding, NTP stratum — because those are the ones whose failure you notice last.
items.install: docker run -d -p 3001:3001 -v uptime-kuma:/app/data louislam/uptime-kuma

items.name: age
items.does: File encryption with small public keys, one obvious command line and no configuration or key ring to maintain.
items.why: The right tool for the archive layer: encrypting a tarball before it goes to an M-DISC or a cold drive should be one command that will still be one command in ten years. GnuPG can do this and also four hundred other things, and its complexity is how people end up with an archive they cannot open. Whatever you choose, the recipient key belongs on paper in the safe — an offline plan that loses its keys is worse than no plan.
items.install: age-keygen -o key.txt   then age -R recipients.txt -o archive.tar.age archive.tar

alts.note: universal and expected by others; far more ways to get it wrong

items.name: CrowdSec
items.does: Parses logs for attack patterns and pushes decisions to a bouncer in the firewall or reverse proxy.
items.why: Relevant only to whatever you still expose to the WAN, which in this architecture should be very little. Its selling point is a shared reputation feed, and that feed is exactly the part that stops working offline — the local detection engine keeps banning what it sees, it just no longer knows what the rest of the world is seeing. Judge it on the local half, because that is the half you keep.
items.install: cscli collections install crowdsecurity/nginx && cscli bouncers add caddy
items.escape: Install collections and parsers while online. The engine and its bouncers then run entirely locally; only the community blocklist goes stale.

alts.note: no cloud component whatsoever; that is both the argument for and against it

items.name: KeePassXC
items.does: Desktop password manager over a single encrypted .kdbx file, with no server component at all.
items.why: The one that keeps working when everything else in this list is powered off, because it is a file. Keep the crown-jewel credentials here — the root CA passphrase, the ZFS keys, the registrar login — and let Syncthing move the file between machines. Its weakness is the mirror image of its strength: concurrent edits on two devices create conflicts a server would have resolved for you.
items.install: dnf install keepassxc   (KeePassDX or Strongbox on mobile)

items.name: Vaultwarden
items.does: Compatible reimplementation of the Bitwarden server in Rust, serving the official Bitwarden clients.
items.why: Passwords and TOTP seeds on your own hardware, with clients that already exist for every platform and cache the vault locally so a phone still opens it with the server unreachable. The failure mode to plan for is not a breach, it is a lockout: an encrypted export in the fire safe and the important credentials on paper, because a self-hosted vault whose host is down and whose owner forgot the master password is unrecoverable by design.
items.install: docker run -d -p 8080:80 -v /vw-data:/data vaultwarden/server

items.name: Wazuh
items.does: Agent-based host monitoring: file integrity, log analysis, vulnerability detection and compliance reporting.
items.why: Included because a Mexican clinic being asked to demonstrate controls under LFPDPPP or NOM-024-SSA3 needs evidence, and Wazuh produces it without sending anything to a vendor. Be honest about the weight: the indexer is OpenSearch and wants 4–8 GB of RAM on its own, which at home scale is a large fraction of a node. Below a handful of machines, auditd plus a log review habit is the proportionate answer.
items.install: docker compose from the wazuh-docker single-node deployment
items.escape: The CVE feeds and rulesets update from the internet. Pull them while online; detection rules keep firing offline, they just stop learning about new vulnerabilities.

items.name: ArchiveBox
items.does: Crawls URLs you feed it and stores HTML, a readable version, a PDF, a screenshot and the WARC for each one.
items.why: Kiwix covers the commons; ArchiveBox covers the twenty vendor manuals, datasheets and forum threads that your specific infrastructure depends on. Point it at the bookmark bar and run it monthly. Expect it to be storage-hungry and to fail on heavily scripted sites — a page that only renders through an API call archives as a shell, and you will not notice until you need it, so spot-check what it captured.
items.disk: grows without limit; 200 GB is a realistic first year
items.install: docker compose up -d, then archivebox add < bookmarks.txt
items.escape: Schedule the crawl while you still have a WAN. An archive you planned to build during the outage is not an archive.

items.name: Calibre-Web
items.does: Browser front end over a Calibre library, with OPDS so e-readers and phone apps can browse and download.
items.why: OPDS is the reason to run this rather than a file share: it is the one catalogue protocol every offline reading app already speaks, so a phone on the guest VLAN can pull a book with no account anywhere. Project Gutenberg is about 80 GB, entirely public domain, and legal to redistribute — which makes it the natural first payload for a handout disc.
items.install: lscr.io/linuxserver/calibre-web, pointed at a directory containing metadata.db

alts.note: the actively developed fork; adds ingest and conversion automation
handles books and comics in one app

items.name: Carino Fleet Offline Edition
items.does: The whole carino.systems tool fleet — imaging, metadata, hashing, learning, hardware reference and the rest — as a folder you can serve from a USB stick.
items.why: Included because it is nearly free rather than because it is impressive: every fleet tool is already client-side static with self-hosted fonts, vendored libraries and no CDN, so packaging is the only remaining work. That is the point worth generalising — a tool written without external fetches is offline-ready by accident, and one written with a CDN reference never will be. Listed plainly as the owner's own work; the bootable ISO is a planned artifact, not a download that exists today.
items.install: Clone the fleet repos into one directory and serve it: python3 -m http.server 8080

items.name: DevDocs
items.does: One searchable local copy of the API documentation for hundreds of languages, libraries and tools.
items.why: Programming without the internet is mostly a documentation problem, not a compiler problem. A couple of gigabytes of DevDocs plus the Stack Exchange ZIM covers the overwhelming majority of what you actually look up. Download only the docsets you use — pulling all of them is slow, large, and mostly languages you will never write.
items.install: docker run -d -p 9292:9292 ghcr.io/freecodecamp/devdocs   then thor docs:download <slug>
items.escape: thor docs:download <slug> while online; re-run per docset when you upgrade the underlying library.

alts.note: desktop app, same docset idea, no server to run
already on the box; free and often enough

items.name: Kiwix
items.does: Serves compressed ZIM archives of Wikipedia, Wiktionary, Stack Exchange, Wikivoyage and Wikimed over plain HTTP.
items.why: The single highest value-per-gigabyte item in the plan. Spanish and English Wikipedia with images is roughly 153 GB; the nopic variants are about 60 GB if the pool is tight, and Wikimed is genuinely useful in a clinic rather than a novelty. Full-text search is built in and runs entirely locally, which is what makes it a substitute for searching the web rather than just a pile of HTML.
items.install: kiwix-serve --port 8080 /srv/zim/*.zim   (or ghcr.io/kiwix/kiwix-serve)
items.escape: Nothing breaks when the ZIMs age, they just get wrong. Re-download the sets you actually use once or twice a year and keep the previous copy until the new one verifies.

items.name: Kolibri
items.does: Offline learning platform that serves Khan Academy, PhET and other open curricula with progress tracking per learner.
items.why: This is the piece that makes an offline box interesting to a school or a clinic waiting room rather than only to you. It has real user accounts, coach reports and a class model — an actual LMS, not a folder of videos. If nobody in the building is studying anything, skip it; fifty gigabytes of curriculum nobody opens is fifty gigabytes.
items.install: pip install kolibri && kolibri start
items.escape: Import channels from Kolibri Studio while online, or sideload the channel database from a USB drive — the sideload path is designed for exactly this and works with no WAN at all.

items.name: Paperless-ngx
items.does: Scans, OCRs, tags and full-text-indexes every document you own, from invoices to equipment manuals.
items.why: Under a Mexican audit or a warranty claim, the question is never whether you have the document — it is whether you can find it in two minutes. Paperless answers that offline, and the OCR runs locally with Tesseract, so nothing goes to a cloud OCR endpoint. Set the language to spa+eng at install; retrofitting OCR language onto ten thousand already-ingested documents is a re-run you will resent.
items.install: ghcr.io/paperless-ngx/paperless-ngx with redis and postgres sidecars

items.name: Protomaps / PMTiles
items.does: Serves vector map tiles for a whole country out of a single static file, readable by MapLibre in any browser.
items.why: One file, no tile server, no database — the full-planet Protomaps basemap is on the order of 120 GB at z0-15, and a country extract of Mexico is a few gigabytes of that, small enough to serve from the same static web server as everything else or read straight off a USB stick by range requests. That single-file property is what makes maps sneakernet-able; a PostGIS-backed tile stack is not something you hand to someone on a disc.
items.disk: a few GB for a Mexico extract; ~120 GB for the whole planet at z0-15
items.install: pmtiles extract <planet pmtiles URL> mexico.pmtiles --bbox=...   then serve the file over HTTP
items.escape: Cut the country extract while online with pmtiles extract and a bounding box, then treat it as a frozen asset. Roads change slowly; re-cut once a year.

alts.note: more styling control, considerably more infrastructure
on the phone itself; the right answer for people leaving the building

items.name: Audiobookshelf
items.does: Audiobook and podcast server with per-user progress sync and mobile clients that download for listening off-network.
items.why: The download-for-offline behaviour in its apps is the point — this is the only media category people consume while physically away from your LAN, so the sync model has to survive leaving the building and coming back. Its podcast fetcher is the one part that needs a WAN; the library itself does not care.
items.install: docker run -d -p 13378:80 -v /audiobooks:/audiobooks ghcr.io/advplyr/audiobookshelf

items.name: Immich
items.does: Photo and video backup for phones, with albums, face grouping, and machine-learning search that runs on your hardware.
items.why: The credible replacement for Google Photos, and the one service in this list where the migration is genuinely urgent — every day you wait is another few hundred photos in someone else's account. Two warnings that matter: it is still pre-1.0 in posture and ships breaking changes, so pin the version and read the release notes; and it is not a backup, so the ZFS dataset it lives on must be in the restic set.
items.ram: 4 GB (6 GB with machine learning enabled)
items.install: docker compose up -d using the upstream docker-compose.yml and .env

alts.note: more stable release cadence, weaker mobile backup

items.name: Jellyfin
items.does: Video library server with hardware transcoding, clients for TV boxes, phones and browsers, and no account of any kind.
items.why: Choose it over Plex specifically because there is no sign-in server to fail: Plex authenticates through plex.tv, and a Plex box behind a dead WAN can lock out the people standing in front of it. Jellyfin's clients are rougher and its metadata scrapers need the internet to fetch artwork. Accept both; artwork is cosmetic, an authentication outage is not.
items.install: docker run -d -p 8096:8096 -v /config:/config -v /media:/media --device /dev/dri jellyfin/jellyfin

items.name: Komga
items.does: Comic, manga and magazine server for CBZ/CBR/PDF, with an OPDS feed and a decent built-in reader.
items.why: Chosen over Kavita for being a single JVM process with no database to administer and an OPDS-PSE feed that page-streams properly to tablet readers. Its metadata scrapers are deliberately minimal, which in an offline context is a feature: nothing in the read path phones anywhere.
items.install: docker run -d -p 25600:25600 -v /comics:/data gotson/komga

alts.note: books and comics in one app, heavier scan pipeline

items.name: Navidrome
items.does: Music server speaking the Subsonic API, so dozens of existing mobile clients work against it unmodified.
items.why: The Subsonic API is the reason: it is an old, boring, widely implemented protocol, which means the phone app that caches an album for the bus already exists and does not care that your server is on 10.20.0.0/24. A single Go binary with a SQLite database, comfortable on a Raspberry Pi, and it will happily index a library the size of a hundred thousand tracks.
items.install: docker run -d -p 4533:4533 -v /music:/music:ro -v /data:/data deluan/navidrome

items.name: Nextcloud
items.does: Files, calendars and contacts over WebDAV, CalDAV and CardDAV, which is what actually decouples a phone from Google.
items.why: Recommended for exactly two apps — Calendar and Contacts — because CalDAV and CardDAV are the only open standards phones still speak natively, and losing your address book to an account lockout is the failure that hurts most. The file sync is slower and heavier than Syncthing and the app ecosystem invites a sprawl of half-maintained plugins; install nothing you cannot name a use for.
items.install: docker run -d -p 8080:80 -v nextcloud:/var/www/html nextcloud   (add postgres and redis for anything real)

alts.note: CalDAV/CardDAV only, ~30 MB of Python, no web UI to maintain

items.name: Plex
items.does: Polished media server whose clients authenticate through plex.tv before they will play your files.
items.why: Listed as a warning, not a recommendation. The apps are better than Jellyfin's and the transcoding is more reliable, and none of that matters the morning the WAN is down and the TV app refuses to sign in. It is the clearest example in this whole document of the pattern to avoid: a local server with a remote dependency welded into the login path, on hardware you own, holding files you own.
items.escape: A server claimed while online keeps serving already-signed-in clients on the LAN for a while, and Plex Pass holders can enable a local-network exception — but every one of those is a vendor policy that can change in an update, not a property of the software. If the files matter, run Jellyfin.

alts.note: the fork of the fork, with no account server anywhere in the path

items.name: 0 A.D.
items.does: Free real-time strategy game in the Age of Empires lineage, with LAN multiplayer over local discovery.
items.why: Stands in here for the whole libre LAN catalogue, which is the only category of game with no DRM story to worry about at all — you copy the installer to a USB stick and it works forever. Note one practical limit before planning a tournament: matches are hosted by a player's client, not a dedicated server, so whoever hosts must stay in the game.
items.install: dnf install 0ad   (or the AppImage/installer from the site)

alts.note: dedicated server, tiny footprint, runs for years
fast arena shooter with a real dedicated server
turn-based, plays fine over a 2 Mbit link
the one that works for children and guests

items.name: Factorio (headless server)
items.does: Dedicated server binary for Factorio, distributed as a plain tarball with no launcher and no runtime licence check.
items.why: Proprietary but exemplary: the game is sold DRM-free, the headless server is a tarball, and setting require-user-verification to false lets clients join with no contact with the vendor's authentication service. This is what a commercial game that respects offline play looks like, and it is worth naming as the standard other publishers fail to meet.
items.install: ./bin/x64/factorio --start-server save.zip --server-settings server-settings.json

items.name: GOG offline installers
items.does: Sells games as standalone installer files with no DRM, no launcher requirement and no activation.
items.why: The single most offline-friendly source of commercial games that exists, and it should be the default place to buy. The important habit is not buying there — it is downloading the offline installers immediately and archiving them alongside their checksums, because purchase history lives on their servers and your archive lives on your shelf. A game you own but have not downloaded is a game you do not have.
items.install: Download the offline backup installers from the account library, verify, then archive to disc
items.escape: Fetch every purchased installer while online and store the files with SHA256SUMS. After that they need nothing, forever.

alts.note: also DRM-free by default, much smaller catalogue

items.name: LanCache
items.does: Transparent caching proxy for game and platform CDNs: one machine downloads a 120 GB game, every other machine on the LAN gets it at line speed.
items.why: The highest value-per-effort container in the entire plan for anyone with more than one gaming machine. It works by DNS: you point clients at the lancache-dns container, which answers CDN hostnames with the cache's address. That also means it fits the split-horizon design exactly, and it turns a throttled or intermittent WAN into a non-issue for bulk downloads even when nothing is censored. Budget 2–5 TB and put it on spinning disks; it is sequential, large-file traffic.
items.install: lancachenet monolithic + lancache-dns containers; point client DNS at lancache-dns
items.escape: The cache only serves what it has already seen, and most platform clients still want to authenticate before they will install from it. Pre-seed by installing the titles you care about while online.

items.name: Luanti
items.does: Voxel game engine and dedicated server, formerly named Minetest, with games and mods written in Lua.
items.why: The renamed-in-2024 Minetest, and the correct answer if the goal is a permanent building game on the LAN with zero licence friction: no accounts, no authentication server, a server binary of a few megabytes, and clients that run on a ten-year-old laptop. It is not Minecraft and children will tell you so; what it is, is a game server that has never once needed the internet.
items.install: luantiserver --port 30000

items.name: Minecraft (Java server)
items.does: The official Java Edition server jar, which can be told to stop checking player identities against Mojang's session servers.
items.why: Setting online-mode=false in server.properties makes the server join-able with no internet at all — the catch is that it also means the server trusts whatever username a client claims, so it belongs on a trusted VLAN and nowhere else. The harder half is the client: the official launcher only enters offline mode after a successful online login, so keep a launcher that supports offline profiles and keep the version jars cached locally before you need them.
items.install: java -Xmx4G -jar server.jar nogui   with online-mode=false in server.properties
items.escape: online-mode=false on the server, plus a client launcher with genuine offline profile support and the asset/version files already downloaded. Do the caching now, not during the outage.

items.name: RomM
items.does: Catalogues a ROM collection with metadata and box art and plays titles in the browser through a bundled EmulatorJS.
items.why: Turns a directory of your own dumps into something a guest can actually use from a kiosk, with no client install. The metadata scrapers need the WAN, so scrape once and then the library is frozen and self-contained. Legally this only works for media you dumped yourself from cartridges and discs you own — that is a real constraint under the Ley Federal del Derecho de Autor, and it is why this stays off any handout disc.
items.install: docker compose with rommapp/romm and a MariaDB sidecar
items.escape: Run the metadata scrape while online; afterwards the database, art and ROMs are entirely local and the emulator runs in the browser.

alts.note: the browser emulator core on its own, no catalogue, drops into any static site
dedicated box wired to the TV; better on a couch, worse in a browser

items.name: Steam (Offline Mode)
items.does: Runs an already-installed library without a connection, provided it was signed in recently and the individual title has no additional DRM.
items.why: Best-effort, never a foundation. Offline Mode needs a successful online login on that machine reasonably recently, breaks if the client decides it must update, and covers only titles whose own DRM cooperates — anything with a third-party launcher or a companion account on top will refuse regardless. Combine it with LanCache to make the pre-download painless, then assume nothing about it during a long outage.
items.escape: Log in and enter Offline Mode deliberately before the outage, pre-download everything you want, and disable client auto-updates. Where a title exists on GOG, buy it there instead.

items.name: docker-mailserver
items.does: Postfix, Dovecot, SpamAssassin and the rest assembled into one container, configured through a handful of files.
items.why: Internal-only mail is a far easier problem than public mail — no reputation, no SPF politics, no fighting to stay out of a spam folder — and it gives you a working address for every device, cron job and appliance that only knows how to complain by email. Do not talk yourself into also making it your public mail server; that is a different, much less pleasant hobby.
items.install: ghcr.io/docker-mailserver/docker-mailserver with a mailserver.env and setup.sh for accounts

items.name: Matrix Synapse
items.does: Reference Matrix homeserver: rooms, history, end-to-end encryption, file transfer, with Element as the client.
items.why: Federation is what makes Matrix interesting and it is also the part that dies with the WAN — which is fine, because a homeserver whose users are all local does not need to federate at all. Run it closed and it is a complete chat system for the building. Be realistic about cost: Python, Postgres, and enough RAM that it is a poor fit for a Raspberry Pi. If chat is all you need, Prosody does it in a tenth of the resources.
items.install: ghcr.io/element-hq/synapse with a Postgres sidecar; disable federation in homeserver.yaml

alts.note: XMPP, Lua, ~50 MB of RAM; less pretty, dramatically lighter
Rust homeserver, far smaller footprint, fewer features

items.name: Meshtastic
items.does: Encrypted text messaging over a self-forming LoRa radio mesh at 915 MHz, with no infrastructure between nodes.
items.why: The cheapest genuine resilience in this entire document: about 48 USD per node with antenna and enclosure, a few kilometres per hop in line of sight, and it depends on nothing you do not physically hold — no tower, no ISP, no power grid beyond a battery. Set expectations correctly: it is SMS-speed text, hundreds of bytes, not a network. Configure the channel keys and hand out the nodes before you need them, because pairing an unconfigured node during an emergency is exactly the wrong time.
items.install: Flash firmware once via the web flasher or esptool, then configure the channel from the phone app

items.name: Mumble
items.does: Low-latency voice chat server with positional audio and clients on every desktop platform.
items.why: Old, small, and it simply works — a server process measured in megabytes that will carry a dozen people on a Raspberry Pi over the LAN with latency nobody notices. The certificate model is self-signed by design, which fits an internal CA neatly. It is voice only; if you need faces, that is Jitsi and a much larger conversation about WebRTC.
items.install: docker run -d -p 64738:64738/tcp -p 64738:64738/udp mumblevoip/mumble-server

items.name: PairDrop
items.does: Browser-to-browser file transfer between devices on the same network, with nothing to install on either end.
items.why: The answer to a guest who needs to hand you a file and has an iPhone. Self-hosted, it discovers peers on the local network and moves the bytes directly over WebRTC — but a strict LAN needs its own STUN configuration or the connection negotiation quietly falls back to nothing. Test it with the WAN unplugged before you rely on it, which is advice that applies to this entire list.
items.install: lscr.io/linuxserver/pairdrop, served over HTTPS (WebRTC will not run on plain HTTP)

items.name: ComfyUI
items.does: Node-graph interface for local image diffusion models, with every step of the pipeline exposed.
items.why: The honest ranking puts this last among the AI items: it is the one that produces the most visible output and solves the fewest actual problems during an outage. It earns a place for illustration and print work — disc art, labels, signage — that would otherwise mean a subscription and an upload. Its extension ecosystem installs code from arbitrary repositories, which is a real supply-chain surface on a machine you are hardening; pin what you install and stop there.
items.ram: 8 GB VRAM for comfortable SDXL-class work
items.install: git clone, pip install -r requirements.txt, python main.py --listen

items.name: LibreTranslate
items.does: Self-hosted translation API over Argos Translate models, with an HTTP endpoint and a small web UI.
items.why: Machine translation is the least obvious dependency in the pile: it is embedded in browsers, phones and half the tools people use daily, and every one of those routes text to a vendor. Load only the language pairs you use — --load-only es,en keeps the memory footprint sane — and accept that quality sits below the large commercial engines. For understanding a datasheet or drafting an email, that gap does not matter.
items.install: docker run -d -p 5000:5000 libretranslate/libretranslate --load-only es,en

items.name: Ollama
items.does: Runs open-weight language models locally with a simple HTTP API and automatic GPU offload.
items.why: This is the item that turns an archive into a librarian, and on a used 24 GB card it is roughly a 750 USD upgrade that outweighs anything else you could add at that price. A 30B-class model in 4-bit fits in 24 GB and answers well enough to be genuinely useful for code, translation and summarising your own documents. Two caveats stated plainly: quality drops sharply below about 8B, and the model does not know your network — it is a reasoning tool over what you feed it, not an oracle about your infrastructure.
items.ram: 16 GB system; 24 GB VRAM for a 30B-class model at 4-bit
items.disk: ~40 GB for a working set of models
items.install: docker run -d --gpus all -v ollama:/root/.ollama -p 11434:11434 ollama/ollama   then ollama pull <model>

alts.note: no registry, no daemon, more knobs; the one to use if you want full control of quantisation

items.name: Open WebUI
items.does: Chat interface over Ollama with user accounts, document upload and a built-in retrieval pipeline.
items.why: The front end that makes local inference usable by someone who will not touch a terminal, and its RAG feature is the practical way to point a model at your own Paperless archive and notes. Check the licence before you ship it to a client: it stopped being plain MIT in 2025 and now carries a branding-retention clause. It also expects to download an embedding model on first run, so do that before the box is sealed.
items.install: docker run -d -p 3000:8080 -e OLLAMA_BASE_URL=http://ollama:11434 ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main

items.name: Piper
items.does: Fast neural text-to-speech from small ONNX voice models, including Spanish voices, entirely on CPU.
items.why: The counterpart to Whisper and the accessibility half of the offline library: a voice model is tens of megabytes and runs faster than real time on a Raspberry Pi, which is what makes read-aloud practical on a kiosk rather than a demo. It is not expressive and it will not read a novel convincingly. For announcements, alerts and reading a document to someone who cannot see the screen, it is entirely sufficient.
items.install: echo "hola" | piper -m es_MX-voice.onnx -f out.wav

items.name: whisper.cpp
items.does: Speech-to-text transcription from a single C++ binary and one model file, on CPU or GPU.
items.why: Transcription is the highest-value offline AI task after search, because it converts the one media type you cannot grep — recorded speech — into something Paperless can index. large-v3 is about 3 GB and runs at better than real time on a modern CPU, so the GPU is optional here. Spanish accuracy is good; heavily accented or overlapping speech still needs a human pass.
items.install: whisper-cli -m models/ggml-large-v3.bin -l es -f audio.wav

items.name: Carino PACS
items.does: Store-and-forward DICOM gateway: receives studies, auto-forwards from watched folders, serves a worklist, takes HL7 orders and holds everything when the primary archive is unreachable.
items.why: Listed plainly as the owner's own project, included because it targets a failure this list otherwise ignores: the archive is down and the scanner is still scanning. It holds the studies, keeps the worklist answering so the technologist can keep working, and back-fills the primary when it returns — and it captures modalities whose only output is a film printer, which are still in service in Mexican clinics. Python and pynetdicom, one JSON configuration file, and no internet in any code path. It is not a diagnostic device and is not for primary interpretation.
items.install: git clone https://github.com/MiguelCarino/Carino-PACS && docker compose up -d

items.name: dcm4chee-arc-light
items.does: Full enterprise DICOM archive: IOCM, HL7 integration, modality worklist, retention policies and audit logging.
items.why: What you deploy when Orthanc is genuinely outgrown, and not before. It is a Java EE application with PostgreSQL and an LDAP configuration store behind it, which means real capability and real operational cost — the configuration lives in LDAP, so backing it up is not the same task as backing up the images. The audit trail is the reason a hospital picks it and the reason it survives an inspection.
items.install: docker compose with dcm4che/dcm4chee-arc-psql, a PostgreSQL and an LDAP container

items.name: OHIF Viewer
items.does: Browser-based DICOM viewer that reads studies from any DICOMweb endpoint, served as static files.
items.why: Static HTML and JavaScript over DICOMweb means it deploys the same way the rest of this fleet does — copy the build directory behind the reverse proxy, point it at Orthanc, done. That makes it the right viewer for a referring physician or a kiosk, where installing a desktop application is not going to happen. For primary diagnosis, use a calibrated workstation and a validated viewer; a browser on an uncalibrated monitor is not that.
items.install: Serve the built static bundle and set the DICOMweb data source to your Orthanc

items.name: OpenEMR
items.does: Full electronic medical record with scheduling, encounters, prescriptions and billing, self-hosted on LAMP.
items.why: The records half of the clinic problem, and the half that decides whether the practice can keep working through an outage — a PACS with no worklist and no patient context is an image archive, not a workflow. It is an old, large PHP codebase and it shows; budget time for configuration rather than expecting an install to be a deployment. Its Mexican localisation is partial, so verify what CFDI and NOM-024 reporting you actually need before committing.
items.install: docker compose with openemr/openemr and a MariaDB sidecar

items.name: Orthanc
items.does: Lightweight DICOM server with storage, query/retrieve, DICOMweb and a plugin API, in one binary plus SQLite.
items.why: The right starting point for a clinic-scale PACS: it installs in an afternoon, runs on a mini-PC, and speaks enough DICOM to talk to equipment that has not been updated since 2011. It has always been an offline system — there is no cloud component to disable — which is why an air-gapped VLAN 99 deployment is the normal configuration rather than a special one. Its own guidance is to move off SQLite to PostgreSQL once the archive is large; take that seriously before you have a million instances.
items.install: docker run -d -p 4242:4242 -p 8042:8042 -v /orthanc-db:/var/lib/orthanc/db orthancteam/orthanc

items.name: Weasis
items.does: Desktop DICOM viewer with multiplanar reconstruction, measurement tools and DICOM send, launchable from an archive.
items.why: The viewer to install on the workstation where someone actually reads studies, and the one that works from a CD handed over by another hospital — which is still how imaging moves between institutions in Mexico. It is Java, so it runs identically on the Windows machine in the reading room and the Linux one in the office, and it needs nothing from the network once installed.
items.install: Install the native package, or launch from Orthanc via the DICOMweb link
